title: Transport across the cell membrane
summary: How do substances get in and out through the membrane, and when is energy needed?
cards.0.p: The cell membrane is made of a double layer of phospholipids, with proteins and carbohydrates among them. The parts of the membrane can slide sideways. That is why the membrane is fluid. Because different parts sit side by side, it is also a mosaic.
cards.0.key: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972. Animal cell membranes also contain cholesterol.
cards.1.p: The membrane is selectively permeable. Small, fat-soluble substances pass straight through it. Glucose and ions pass with the help of membrane proteins. Very large substances are carried in vesicles.
cards.1.key: Small substances like O₂ and CO₂ pass easily. Charged or large substances pass through proteins, and very large ones in vesicles.
cards.2.p: The spontaneous spreading of a substance from where its concentration is high to where it is low is called diffusion. Diffusion uses no ATP. Once the concentrations are equal, net movement stops.
cards.2.key: Diffusion speeds up as temperature, concentration difference and surface area increase. It also speeds up as particles get smaller. O₂ passing into the blood in the lungs is an example.
cards.3.p: Glucose and ions cannot cross the membrane on their own. They still move from high to low, but through channel or carrier proteins. This is called facilitated diffusion, and it uses no ATP.
cards.3.key: Once all the carriers are busy, the rate of movement stops rising.
cards.4.p: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane is called osmosis. Water moves, on balance, from the side with less solute to the side with more solute. In other words, water flows from where water is plentiful to where it is scarce.
cards.4.key: Water crosses the membrane in both directions. Osmosis describes the direction of net flow. Most water passes through channels called aquaporins.
cards.5.p: In a hypotonic environment, water enters the cell. A red blood cell swells and can burst. This is called hemolysis. In an isotonic environment, there is no net water movement. In a hypertonic environment, water leaves the cell and the red blood cell shrinks.
cards.5.svg#9: a red blood cell in three environments
cards.5.key: That is why the saline given through an IV is isotonic and contains 0.9% NaCl.
cards.6.p: A plant cell in a hypotonic environment takes in water and presses against its cell wall. This is called turgor. In a hypertonic environment, it loses water and its membrane pulls away from the wall. This is called plasmolysis. The cell returning to normal in pure water is called deplasmolysis.
cards.6.svg#9: green frame: cell wall · blue: vacuole
cards.6.key: Plants wilt in salty soil because of plasmolysis.
cards.6.once.soru: What happens if we put a plant cell in pure water?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Water flows in, but there is a strong cell wall outside the membrane. The cell presses against the wall, and the wall's resistance stops more water from entering.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: A red blood cell can burst, but a plant cell has a wall outside its membrane.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Pure water is more dilute than the inside of the cell. So water does not leave the cell, it flows in.
cards.7.p: A solution's power to draw water by osmosis is called osmotic pressure, and it rises with concentration. In a plant cell, the suction force is found by subtracting turgor pressure from osmotic pressure.
cards.7.svg#5: as the cell takes in water →
cards.7.key: As the cell takes in water, turgor rises and suction force falls. At full turgor, the suction force is zero.
cards.7.once.soru: Which plant cell draws in water more strongly?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: This cell's inside is concentrated, and the wall does not press on it at all. So its pull for water is highest.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: This cell is full of water, and the wall presses back on it. It can't take in more water.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Both the concentration inside the two cells and the pressure from the wall differ.
cards.8.h: Active transport and the Na-K pump
cards.8.p: Moving a substance from low to high, that is "uphill", is called active transport. It needs a carrier protein and ATP. For example, the Na⁺-K⁺ pump uses each ATP to push 3 Na⁺ ions out and bring 2 K⁺ ions in.
cards.8.key: Passive transport also happens across the membrane of a dead cell, but active transport happens only in living cells. A root taking up minerals from the soil is also active transport.
cards.9.p: Large substances are carried in vesicles made from the membrane, using ATP. Taking substances in is called endocytosis. Taking in solids is phagocytosis, and taking in fluids is pinocytosis. Sending substances out is called exocytosis.
cards.9.svg#8: Top: outside the cell · Bottom: inside the cell · ATP is used
cards.9.key: Insulin secretion is an example of exocytosis. Exocytosis enlarges the membrane, and endocytosis shrinks it. Transport by vesicles happens only in living cells.
cards.9.once.soru: How does a white blood cell take in a bacterium?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.yazi: It wraps it in membrane, in a vesicle
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: A bacterium is too big to pass through any channel. The white blood cell wraps it in membrane and takes it in inside a vesicle.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Channels are for small particles such as ions and water. A bacterium is much bigger.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Only small particles cross the membrane by diffusion. A bacterium can't seep through.
cards.10.p:
• The membrane has a fluid mosaic structure and is selectively permeable.
• Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive transport. Substances move from high to low, and no ATP is used.
• In active transport, substances are moved from low to high. Proteins and ATP are needed.
• Large substances are carried in vesicles by endocytosis and exocytosis.
quiz.0.q: Which kinds of transport use ATP? Put each one in the right group.
quiz.0.e: Diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion happen on their own, from high to low. The Na-K pump moves substances from low to high, and phagocytosis and exocytosis form vesicles. These three use ATP.
quiz.1.q: A plant cell has an osmotic pressure of 12 atm and a turgor pressure of 5 atm. What is its suction force in atm?
quiz.1.e: Suction force is osmotic pressure minus turgor pressure: 12 − 5 = 7 atm. As the cell takes in water, turgor rises and suction force falls.
quiz.2.q: Put in order what happens to a plant cell placed in salt water.
quiz.2.ogeler.0: The outside becomes hypertonic to the cell
quiz.2.ogeler.1: Water leaves the vacuole by osmosis
quiz.2.ogeler.2: The vacuole shrinks and turgor pressure drops
quiz.2.ogeler.3: The membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis)
quiz.2.e: When the outside is more concentrated, water leaves the cell, the vacuole shrinks and turgor is lost. Finally the membrane pulls away from the wall. If the cell is put in pure water, the process reverses. This is called deplasmolysis.
quiz.3.q: Match each event with its kind of transport.
quiz.3.ciftler.0.0: A white blood cell engulfing a bacterium
quiz.3.ciftler.1.0: A cell taking in a fluid droplet
quiz.3.e: Engulfing a solid particle is called phagocytosis, and taking in a fluid droplet is called pinocytosis. A vesicle fusing with the membrane and emptying its contents is called exocytosis. The diffusion of water across the membrane is osmosis.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Send particles to the membrane and put a red blood cell in different waters.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Look at the heads and tails of the phospholipids in the membrane.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which part of the phospholipids faces the water on both sides of the membrane?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A phospholipid's head is water-loving (hydrophilic), and its tails are water-avoiding (hydrophobic). So the heads face outward, toward the water on both sides. The tails face inward, toward each other.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The tails are like oil and avoid water. Notice where the tails point in the picture.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Look at the picture: both layers have the same arrangement. The water-loving part always turns toward water.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Tap the particles on the left and send each one to the membrane. See which ones can pass and how.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: Small, uncharged O₂ passed straight between the phospholipids.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: Glucose couldn't pass through the oily layer. It passed through a carrier protein in the membrane.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Send the protein to the membrane
A:adimlar.1.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: The protein is too big to pass either between the phospholipids or through the carrier. Large substances like this are carried in vesicles.
A:adimlar.2.metin: There are different numbers of oxygen (O₂) molecules on the two sides of the membrane. Small, uncharged O₂ molecules can easily pass between the phospholipids.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What do you think happens when you press play?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: They move from the crowded side to the other, and the numbers even out
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Particles are always moving, and more of them hit and cross the membrane from the side where they are crowded. Once the numbers are equal, crossing continues both ways, but net movement stops.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: They move from the sparse side to the crowded side
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: This doesn't happen on its own. It needs energy, as you will see in later steps.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: O₂ is small and uncharged, so it can cross the membrane.
A:adimlar.3.metin: On the left of the membrane are O₂ molecules and Na⁺ ions, all moving randomly all the time. Watch the counts and the crossings. If needed, put a channel protein in the membrane or refill the container.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Watch O₂ even out on both sides. Do the molecules stop once they're even?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: O₂ spread from where it was crowded to where it was sparse. This is called diffusion, and no ATP is used. Once even, the molecules still cross, but about equally in both directions, so net movement stopped.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Get Na⁺ ions to the right of the membrane.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: Charged Na⁺ ions can't pass through the oily middle of the phospholipids. When the channel protein opened, they moved from high to low, again with no ATP used. This is called facilitated diffusion.
A:adimlar.4.metin: The inside of a red blood cell is like 0.9% salt water. Now we will put the red blood cell in pure water.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What happens to the red blood cell in pure water?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: There is no solute outside, and water is plentiful. So water moves, on balance, into the red blood cell, and the cell swells. If it swells too much, it can burst.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: For it to shrink, water would have to leave. But water moves from where it is plentiful to where it is scarce.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The inside and outside of the cell have different concentrations. Water flows in the direction that evens out this difference.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Now you set it. Make the outside salty enough for the red blood cell to lose water and shrink.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: The outside is now saltier than the inside of the cell. This is called a hypertonic environment. Water leaves the cell, and the red blood cell shrinks.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A cell keeps far more potassium (K⁺) ions inside than outside. Pump proteins in the membrane make this possible.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: The pump will move K⁺ ions from where they are few to where they are many. What does this need?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Moving a substance from where it is scarce to where it is plentiful is like pushing something uphill. ATP supplies the energy needed.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Spontaneous movement is always from high to low. Here the direction is the opposite.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A channel only opens a door. Particles still move from high to low.
A:kapanis.0: The cell membrane is made of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating in it. This is called the fluid mosaic model.
A:kapanis.1: In diffusion, particles move from high to low without using energy. Small, uncharged particles pass straight through the membrane.
A:kapanis.2: In facilitated diffusion, particles such as ions move through channel or carrier proteins, still from high to low.
A:kapanis.3: In active transport, pump proteins use ATP and move particles from low to high.
A:kapanis.4: In osmosis, water moves from a less salty environment to a saltier one. A red blood cell swells in a hypotonic environment and shrinks in a hypertonic one.
